processing: A whole-leaf green tea from the Nilgiri hills: the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried. Methods vary by estate and small grower.
harvest_season: Little is recorded on a prized green tea season. The Nilgiris pick much of the year, and estates set their own timing.
appearance_dry: Whole or broken twisted leaf, olive to dark green, as is usual for Indian orthodox greens.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green to light gold and clear, typical of Indian orthodox greens.
appearance_wet: Whole leaves or large pieces in a dull green, typical of orthodox green tea.
taste_profile: One taster of an organic estate lot found it tangy and fresh, with lemon or lime, grass and cooked vegetables on the nose; lots differ a good deal by estate.

brewing.notes: Usually brewed Western style. If it tastes bland, go hotter and longer rather than adding more leaf.

vintage_note: Sold by estate or grower, usually without a vintage or a famous picking. As with other green teas, buy the most recent harvest available and drink it within about a year; a stated pick date is a good sign.
description:
Most people know the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu for fragrant black tea, but the hills have also made green tea for decades. It is made as whole leaf, and the EU is the main export market for it.

The tea grows on high slopes, with the district ranging from about 900 to 2,600 metres. Beyond killing the green and rolling, there is no single regional method. Larger estates and small growers each work in their own way.

The character is less settled than a famous Chinese green. One reviewer of an organic estate lot found citrus, grass and cooked vegetables, liked the fresh tang, yet found the whole thing a little grey. Their best cup came from a single long steep at fairly hot water; cooler water made it bland.

Buy by name: an estate or grower and a recent pick date say much more than the word Nilgiri on its own. Try two estates before forming an opinion of the region.
history:
Green tea has been made in the Nilgiris since 1969, according to trade reporting on the region, and it has stayed in production alongside the main orthodox black and machine-made teas.

Small growers have also moved into specialty tea more recently: one, Prabhu Nanjan, started around 2014.
